tip: 'Dont' means "whose" here, and French keeps the article: 'dont la culture' = "whose culture". You never drop the 'la' the way English drops "the".
French drops "a" before a job after 'être': 'est pilote' = "is a pilot", not 'est un pilote'. The article usually returns when you describe the job.
Information is usually plural in French: 'les informations... sont' takes a plural verb, while English keeps "information is" singular and uncountable.
'Dont' stands in for a 'de' phrase: 'il est le directeur de l'entreprise' becomes 'l'entreprise dont il est le directeur'.
That 'ne' after 'craindre' isn't a negation: 'qu'elle ne mourût' means fearing she WOULD die, not that she wouldn't.
'Or' at the start of a sentence means "now" or "however" – it introduces a new, often contradictory fact.
'Fît' is bookish – the literary past subjunctive. Spoken French reaches for the present instead: 'il fallait que chacun fasse sa part'.
English says "as soon as it has arrived", but French uses the future after 'dès que' when the main clause is future: 'dès que le colis sera arrivé'.
'Leur' here means "to them", not just "them": 'nous leur avons laissé' = we left a message TO them. It's the give-to pronoun, distinct from 'les' (plain "them").
'Vînt' looks like a typo but it's the imperfect subjunctive, a literary tense. In everyday speech you'd just say 'qu'elle vienne me voir'.
'Eût oublié' is a literary form: everyday French would say 'il semblait qu'il ait oublié'. Same meaning, bookish flavour.
'Quand bien même' = "even if", but unlike 'si' it takes the conditional: 'quand bien même il aurait raison' = even if he were right.
'Avoir beau' + verb has nothing to do with beauty: 'on a beau chercher' means "no matter how hard we search". It sets up wasted effort, then the letdown.
One word or two flips the meaning: 'quoique' (one word, as here) = "although"; 'quoi que' (two words) = "whatever". 'Quoique la nuit fût sombre' = although the night was dark.
After 'le seul ... qui', French usually switches to the subjunctive: 'le seul homme qui eût du courage'. The claim reads as a judgement, not plain fact.
French uses 'faire' for the state of the sky: 'il fait nuit' means "it's dark", literally "it makes night". That's why the verb here shows up as 'fît'.
The 'ne' in 'avant que le soleil ne se couchât' isn't a negation – it's a decorative 'ne' that 'avant que' attracts. The sun still sets.
'Même si' = "even if", yet it takes the plain imperfect, never the subjunctive: 'même si tu me suppliais'. (Contrast 'bien que', which does.)
'Mettre du sien' means to pull your weight, literally "to put some of one's own". 'Chacun y mette du sien' = everyone pitches in.
'On dirait' is literally "one would say", but it means "it looks like". 'On dirait qu'il va pleuvoir' = the sky looks like rain – nobody is actually speaking.
Tucked inside a sentence, a question normally keeps plain word order – no inversion: 'où j'habitais', not 'où habitais-je': 'elle a voulu savoir où j'habitais'.
French changes an opinion, not a mind: 'changer d'avis' is literally "change of opinion", with no possessive word. 'Qu'elle ait changé d'avis' = that she changed her mind.
'Si j'étais toi' uses the imperfect after 'si' for a present hypothetical – in these if-sentences French avoids the conditional right after 'si'.
'Faire' + infinitive = make someone do something, and the doer follows the pair: 'a fait travailler les élèves' – literally "made work the students".
'Quand bien même' means "even if", but it takes the conditional, not the subjunctive you might expect here: 'quand bien même cela serait possible' ('serait' = would be).
French switches to the subjunctive when the thing you want may not exist yet: 'un livre qui soit intéressant' uses 'soit', not 'est' – any such book, not one specific one.
'Pour peu que' means "if ... at all": 'pour peu qu'il fasse un effort' = if he makes even the slightest effort. It takes the subjunctive, hence 'fasse'.
The 'n'' in 'vous n'ayez' is not a negative: it's a bare 'ne' that 'à moins que' attracts. The meaning is unless you have a better idea, not unless you don't.
'Il vous suffit de' is impersonal – literally "it suffices to you" = all you have to do is. 'Il vous suffit de signer' = you just need to sign, nothing more.
In the passive the participle quietly agrees: 'peints' takes -s to match 'ces tableaux' – a match English has no way to show.
